title: A modular toolkit for synchronized multimodal data acquisition in systems neuroscience
author: Xiaoyue Mike Zheng
materials: Basic software setup Before setting up the acquisition workflow, install and configure a few basic development tools on the Windows acquisition computer: Visual Studio Code for editing code and configuration files Git for working with the repository Miniconda for creating the Python environment used by the acquisition scripts Additional device-specific software will be installed in the sections where each modality is configured. For this protocol, users should be comfortable with basic command-line navigation and commands as they go, whether in Bash, Windows PowerShell, or a similar shell. For conda-specific commands, the official conda cheatsheet is a useful quick reference.

Set up the Avisoft audio hardware In this protocol, we record ultrasonic audio with an Avisoft UltraSoundGate 116H and an Avisoft CM16/CMPA condenser ultrasound microphone. The UltraSoundGate 116H is a single-channel USB recording interface for high-sample-rate ultrasound acquisition, and the CM16/CMPA microphone is designed for ultrasonic recording with broad frequency response and high sensitivity. The 116H also has a TTL-compatible digital input, which we will use to record the Arduino sync pulse train alongside the audio. Connect the CM16/CMPA microphone to the UltraSoundGate 116H using the XLR microphone cable. Mount the microphone in the recording rig so it has a clear acoustic path to the animal or sound source; the microphone is directional, so placement and orientation affect the recorded signal. Place the UltraSoundGate 116H near the sync circuit and somewhere accessible for later gain adjustment. Leave the USB cable disconnected for now; we will connect the 116H to the acquisition computer after installing and configuring the Avisoft recording software. Gain will be adjusted later using the live level display in RECORDER USGH. To route the sync signal into the 116H, connect the Arduino sync output circuit to the 116H digital input using a 2.5 mm mono plug cable, such as Tensility 10-00343 ( Figure 8 ). Use the 116H digital input/DIN connector for this step, not the TRG or SYNC connector. The digital input carries the same sync pulse train used to trigger the camera, allowing RECORDER USGH to store the pulse state in the audio file. For a 2.5 mm mono plug, the tip is normally the signal contact and the sleeve is normally ground; use a multimeter to confirm which cable lead connects to each contact before wiring. Connect the tip/signal lead to the Arduino sync output, and connect the sleeve/ground lead to Arduino GND. Make sure the Arduino and UltraSoundGate digital input share a common ground. This completes the hardware path needed for embedding the sync pulse train in the audio recording. Figure 8. Avisoft audio hardware and sync input wiring The CM16/CMPA microphone is connected to the UltraSoundGate 116H, and the Arduino sync output is routed to the 116H digital input through a 2.5 mm mono plug cable.

Set up the DAQ sync input hardware Before connecting the Arduino sync output to an electrophysiology or DAQ system, check the voltage level expected by the DAQ digital input. The Arduino sync output used here is a 5 V digital signal, while some DAQ inputs expect 3.3 V logic. For this protocol, we step the Arduino sync signal down to approximately 3.3 V before routing it to the DAQ digital input. Build a simple voltage divider on the breadboard using two resistors with a 1:2 ratio, for example 1.1 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ. Connect the Arduino sync output to the 1.1 kΩ resistor, connect the other end of that resistor to the divider output node, and connect the 2.2 kΩ resistor from that node to ground. Connect the divider output node to the DAQ digital input channel. With this resistor ratio, a 5 V Arduino pulse is reduced to approximately 3.3 V at the divider output. Connect Arduino GND to the DAQ ground so the two devices share a common voltage reference. This common ground is required for the DAQ input to interpret the sync pulse correctly. The final wiring is therefore: Arduino sync output -> voltage divider -> DAQ digital input, with Arduino GND connected to DAQ GND ( Figure 11 ). Figure 11. Voltage-divided sync input for DAQ recording The Arduino sync pulse is reduced from 5 V to approximately 3.3 V with a resistor divider, then routed to a DAQ digital input channel. Arduino GND and DAQ GND are connected to provide a common reference.

steps.title: Clone the repository
steps.instruction: Open an Anaconda PowerShell Prompt, navigate to the folder where the code will reside, create a Projects directory, and clone the multimodal‑sync‑toolkit repository from GitHub, logging in if prompted.

substeps.instruction: mkdir ~/Projects
cd ~/Projects
git clone https://github.com/xmikezheng20/multimodal-sync-toolkit.git

steps.title: Prepare Arduino hardware and test circuit
steps.instruction: Gather an Arduino Mega 2560 Rev3 (or compatible board) and a basic electronics starter kit, then build a visual test circuit using digital pin 11, a current‑limiting resistor, an LED, and Arduino GND; the LED will indicate the sync pulse train.

substeps.instruction: Connect pin 11 to a resistor, then to the LED long leg.
Connect the LED short leg to Arduino GND.
Optionally connect the output and ground to an oscilloscope for waveform inspection.

steps.title: Upload and test Arduino sync firmware
steps.instruction: Load the sync pulse generator sketch, temporarily replace the microsecond delays with a 1‑second delay for visual testing, upload, verify start/stop via the Serial Monitor, then restore the original timing and re‑upload.

substeps.instruction: Open Arduino IDE and load acquisition/arduino/sync_pulse_generator/sync_pulse_generator.ino.
Replace delayMicroseconds(pulseHighUs) and delayMicroseconds(pulseLowUs) with delay(1000) for a slow blink.
Select Board = Arduino Mega 2560 Rev3 and the correct COM port (e.g., COM3).
Upload the modified sketch.
Open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud, send "1" → LED blinks once per second, send "0" → LED off.
Re‑edit the sketch to restore delayMicroseconds(pulseHighUs) and delayMicroseconds(pulseLowUs).
Upload the original sketch again; at the default 50 Hz sync rate the LED stays continuously on while the pulse train runs.

steps.title: Install and configure Bonsai for pulse control
steps.instruction: Download and install Bonsai, add the Starter Pack, open the simple pulse‑control workflow, set the serial port to match the Arduino, and test start/stop via keyboard keys.

substeps.instruction: Install Bonsai from the Windows Start menu.
In Bonsai → Manage Packages, install the Bonsai Starter Pack.
Open acquisition/bonsai/workflows/simple_pulse_control.bonsai.
Edit both SerialWriteLine nodes so PortName matches the Arduino COM port (e.g., COM3).
Close the Arduino Serial Monitor to free the port.
Run the workflow (Start button), click inside the window, press T → LED turns on, press F → LED turns off, then click Stop.

steps.title: Set up FLIR camera and wiring
steps.instruction: Mount a FLIR Blackfly S BFS‑U3‑20S4M‑C monochrome USB3 camera with a 4.5 mm C‑mount lens (Edmund Optics #86‑900), attach its GPIO cable, and wire the Arduino sync output to the camera trigger input according to the Teledyne guide.

substeps.instruction: Mount camera and lens in the behavioral rig.
Leave the USB cable unplugged for now.
Connect Arduino digital pin 11 (sync output) to the green wire of the camera GPIO cable.
Connect Arduino GND to the brown wire of the camera GPIO cable.
Verify wiring against the camera’s pinout before proceeding.

steps.title: Install Spinnaker SDK and configure camera
steps.instruction: Install Windows 64‑bit Spinnaker SDK 1.29.0.5 and Bonsai.Spinnaker 0.7.1, then use SpinView to set manual acquisition parameters, disable auto‑exposure/gain, select Mono8 pixel format, and configure hardware triggering on Line 3 with rising‑edge trigger mode.

substeps.instruction: Download Spinnaker SDK 1.29.0.5 (Application Development install).
Install Bonsai.Spinnaker 0.7.1 (compatible with the SDK).
Connect the camera via USB3 and launch SpinView.
Start free‑run streaming (trigger off) to adjust focus, Exposure Time, Gain, Gamma, and verify Device Link Throughput Limit is sufficient.
Disable Automatic Exposure and Gain; set manual Exposure Time and Gain for the experiment.
In Image Format tab, set Pixel Format = Mono8.
In GPIO tab, set Trigger Source = Line 3, Trigger Overlap = Read Out, Trigger Mode = On.
Test: with Arduino pulse off no frames appear; press T in Bonsai to start pulse → frames appear at 50 Hz; press F → frames freeze.
Save the configuration as a camera settings profile.

steps.title: Monitor triggered video in Bonsai
steps.instruction: Install the Bonsai.Spinnaker package, open the triggered‑video‑monitor workflow, set the camera SerialNumber and COM port, then verify that video frames appear only when the Arduino pulse train is running.

substeps.instruction: In Bonsai Manage Packages, install Bonsai.Spinnaker 0.7.1.
Open acquisition/bonsai/workflows/triggered_video_monitor_v1.bonsai.
Set SerialNumber to match the camera shown in SpinView.
Set ColorProcessing = NoColorProcessing.
Confirm COM port matches the Arduino (e.g., COM3).
Run the workflow, press T → video updates, press F → video freezes, then Stop.

steps.title: Create acquisition Conda environment
steps.instruction: From an Anaconda PowerShell Prompt, create and activate the multimodal‑sync‑acquisition environment using the provided YAML file; optionally create the legacy ffmpeg environment if needed.

substeps.instruction: cd to the repository root.
conda env create --prefix $HOME/.conda/envs/multimodal-sync-acquisition -f acquisition/envs/acquisition.yaml
conda activate $HOME/.conda/envs/multimodal-sync-acquisition
Optional: conda env create --prefix $HOME/.conda/envs/multimodal-sync-acquisition -f acquisition/envs/acquisition_legacy_ffmpeg422.yaml

steps.title: Review config, workflow, and wrapper
steps.instruction: Open the example YAML config (example_v1_50hz.yaml) and verify that sync_rate_hz = 50, paths to output folder, Bonsai executable, and workflow are correct, and that video frame size, pixel format, ffmpeg options (preset:p4, pix_fmt:yuv420p), pipe name, and segmentation settings match the intended acquisition.

substeps.instruction: Inspect acquisition/configs/example_v1_50hz.yaml.
Confirm session.sync_rate_hz = 50.
Check paths: output folder, Bonsai executable, workflow (triggered_video_writer_v1.bonsai).
Verify video.ffmpeg_output_options includes preset:p4 and pix_fmt:yuv420p.
Ensure pipe_name = "\\.\pipe\videopipe1".

steps.title: Run acquisition wrapper and record video
steps.instruction: With the acquisition environment active, launch the Python acquisition wrapper, verify printed settings, start the Arduino pulse train via Bonsai (T/F keys), and let ffmpeg encode the triggered frames to an MP4 file.

substeps.instruction: python acquisition/scripts/run_acquisition.py -c acquisition/configs/example_v1_50hz.yaml
Confirm camera serial number, Bonsai path, output folder, and pipe name in the terminal output.
When Bonsai window opens, ensure no image appears (pulse off).
Press T in Bonsai → Arduino pulse train starts, LED on, video updates.
Press F in Bonsai → pulse train stops, video freezes.
Click Stop in Bonsai to close the workflow.
The Python script ends and ffmpeg finalizes cam0_*.mp4 in the configured output folder.

steps.title: Configure Avisoft RECORDER USGH for audio sync
steps.instruction: Install Avisoft RECORDER USGH, connect the UltraSoundGate 116H, set a base directory, permanent trigger mode with zero pre/post‑trigger, sampling rate 250 kHz, 16‑bit WAV format, enable Keep DIN and Show DIN, use date‑based compact filenames, and set maximum file length to 60 minutes.

substeps.instruction: Install RECORDER USGH and optionally SASLab Lite.
Connect UltraSoundGate 116H via USB and open RECORDER.
Options → Configuration → Channel Settings: set base directory.
Trigger Settings: mode = permanent, pre‑trigger = 0, post‑trigger = 0.
Input Device Settings: select UltraSoundGate 116H, Sampling Rate = 250 kHz, Recording Format = 16‑bit WAV.
Device Settings: enable Keep DIN, Show DIN, ignore GetOverlappedResult error.
Filenames: enable date‑based filenames, compact format.
Maximum file size/length: set to 60 minutes.
Save configuration.
Adjust microphone gain to avoid clipping and keep it fixed.

steps.title: Record audio with embedded sync pulse
steps.instruction: Start RECORDER USGH recording first, then start the Arduino sync pulse train (via Bonsai or Arduino Serial Monitor), stop the pulse train, and finally stop the audio recording, ensuring the full pulse train is sandwiched inside the WAV file.

substeps.instruction: In RECORDER USGH, click Start to begin file writing.
Start the Arduino pulse train (press T in Bonsai or send "1" from Serial Monitor).
Observe LED on and DIN indicator toggling in RECORDER.
When the session is complete, press F in Bonsai (or send "0") to stop the pulse train; LED turns off.
Stop RECORDER recording.

steps.title: Visualize embedded audio LSB sync
steps.instruction: Activate the sync_analysis Conda environment and run the Jupyter notebook inspect_audio_lsb_sync.ipynb on the recorded WAV file to extract and plot the least‑significant‑bit sync track.

substeps.instruction: conda activate $HOME/.conda/envs/multimodal-sync-analysis
Launch Jupyter and open sync_analysis/notebooks/inspect_audio_lsb_sync.ipynb
Run the notebook cells to load the WAV, extract LSB, and display the waveform with the sync train.

steps.title: Configure Intan RHX for sync input
steps.instruction: Install the Intan RHX software, connect the RHD USB board, set acquisition sampling rate to 30 kHz, choose One File Per Signal Type format, enable the digital input channel wired to the Arduino sync output, and save the settings as an XML file.

substeps.instruction: Install Intan RHX software from the Intan website.
Connect RHD USB interface and power it on.
Open RHX, verify board detection.
Set Sampling Rate = 30.0 kHz.
Set File Format = One File Per Signal Type.
Enable the digital input channel that receives the Arduino sync pulse; verify state changes when pulse train runs.
Save the configuration as an XML file.

steps.title: Record Intan data with embedded sync
steps.instruction: Start Intan recording, then start the Arduino pulse train, stop the pulse train, and finally stop Intan recording, ensuring the full pulse train is captured on the digital input channel.

substeps.instruction: In RHX, click Start Recording and confirm files are being written.
Start the Arduino pulse train (press T in Bonsai or send "1" from Serial Monitor).
LED on and digital input toggles.
Press F to stop the pulse train; LED off.
Stop RHX recording.

steps.title: Organize session folder structure
steps.instruction: Create a self‑contained session directory with subfolders for notes, logs, raw data per modality, sync outputs, and processed results; keep raw_ folders read‑only after acquisition.

substeps.instruction: mkdir example_session_01
Create notes.txt and logs/ subfolders.
Create raw_audio/<stream>/, raw_video/<cam>/, raw_intan/ subfolders and copy the respective files.
Create sync/ for validation outputs.
Create processed_audio/, processed_video/, processed_intan/ for downstream analysis results.

steps.title: Validate session data
steps.instruction: Create and activate the analysis environment, then run the validate_session.py script with the session path and appropriate YAML config; confirm that audio, Intan, and video pulse/frame counts match and that validation passes.

substeps.instruction: cd sync_analysis
conda env create --prefix $HOME/.conda/envs/multimodal-sync-analysis -f envs/analysis.yaml
conda activate $HOME/.conda/envs/multimodal-sync-analysis
pip install -e ".[all]"
python sync_analysis/scripts/validate_session.py \
-s /path/to/example_session_01 \
-c /path/to/example_a1v1i_50hz.yaml \
--log-file /path/to/example_session_01/logs/validate_session.log
Check terminal output for matching counts (e.g., audio:c1_high sync_pulses = 1133, intan:0 sync_pulses = 1133, video:cam0 frames = 1133) and for the message "Session validation passed".
Validation results are written to example_session_01/sync/.

steps.title: Map audio and video events to session timebase
steps.instruction: Open the notebook map_buzzer_led_to_session_timebase.ipynb, detect buzzer intervals in audio and LED‑on intervals in video, construct SyncTimebase and FrameTimebase objects using the extracted sync data, map source signals and events to shared session time, and plot them together.

substeps.instruction: Launch Jupyter and open sync_analysis/notebooks/map_buzzer_led_to_session_timebase.ipynb.
Load the audio WAV, compute amplitude, detect buzzer intervals.
Load the video MP4, extract mean intensity from a manually selected LED ROI, detect LED‑on intervals.
Create audio_timebase = SyncTimebase.from_sync_data(audio_sync_data, source_rate_hz=audio_sample_rate_hz, source_index_name="sample").
Create video_timebase = FrameTimebase(sync_rate_hz=50).
Map signals: audio_session_signal = map_source_signal_to_session_time(audio_source_signal, audio_timebase).
Map video: led_session_signal = map_source_signal_to_session_time(led_source_signal, video_timebase).
Map events similarly and plot all on a common session‑time axis to verify alignment.

steps.title: Create synchronized demo video
steps.instruction: Run the make_demo_video.py script with the session path, session config, demo‑video config, and desired clip window; the script renders camera frames and an audio waveform on a shared timeline and encodes them with ffmpeg.

substeps.instruction: python sync_analysis/scripts/make_demo_video.py \
--session /path/to/example_session_01 \
--session-config sync_analysis/configs/example_a1v1i_50hz.yaml \
--demo-video-config sync_analysis/configs/demo_video/example_video_audio_waveform.yaml \
--clip-start-session-s 0 \
--clip-end-session-s 15 \
--output /path/to/example_session_01/demo_videos/demo_video_0_15.mp4

steps.title: Adjust ffmpeg GPU encoding settings (optional)
steps.instruction: If GPU encoding fails or performance is suboptimal, verify that the conda‑forge ffmpeg version (e.g., 8.1.1) works with the installed NVIDIA driver (e.g., 581.57 on RTX 3060) and adjust video.ffmpeg_output_options in the YAML config; for legacy rigs use ffmpeg 4.2.2 with driver 516.94 on RTX 4000.

substeps.instruction: Check GPU model and driver version.
Edit video.ffmpeg_output_options in the acquisition YAML (e.g., add "preset:p4", "pix_fmt:yuv420p").
If needed, create a legacy environment with acquisition_legacy_ffmpeg422.yaml and use the corresponding config.

description: Overview of pulse control In this section, we set up a Windows PC to control the shared synchronization signal used during acquisition. The PC communicates with an Arduino microcontroller over a serial connection, and the Arduino generates the digital pulse train that defines the experimental session timebase. We first test pulse control directly from the Arduino IDE using an LED and an intentionally slow blink pattern, then reproduce the same start/stop control from a simple Bonsai workflow. This provides a minimal working example of serially controlled pulse generation before the same Bonsai control logic is incorporated into the full acquisition workflow. Overview of electrophysiology and I/O acquisition Electrophysiology and other DAQ-based recordings often include continuous neural signals together with auxiliary input channels for behavioral events, stimulation timing, or other external signals. For synchronization, the key requirement is that the DAQ system records the shared sync pulse train in the same timebase as the neural or analog signals. A dedicated digital input channel is well suited for this because each sample of the digital channel records whether the sync line is low or high. In this protocol, we demonstrate this idea with an Intan RHD USB interface board for electrophysiology and general I/O recording. This board has been discontinued, but it remains a useful example of a DAQ system that records amplifier data and digital inputs together. The same synchronization logic can be applied to other acquisition systems, such as the Open Ephys Acquisition Board with I/O hardware, or pyPhotometry for fiber photometry, as long as the system can record an external digital input alongside its primary data stream. Here, we route the Arduino sync pulse train into one DAQ digital input channel.
